required_facts_checked: The study analyzed more than 1,000 AI Engineer job descriptions from Berlin, Amsterdam, London, Los Angeles and New York.
An LLM classified 889 descriptions into AI-first, AI-support and traditional ML/DL categories.
AI-first roles were about 70 percent and involved LLM or GenAI systems, RAG, agents, evaluation and production deployment.
AI-support roles were about 28.5 percent and covered platforms, GPU/inference infrastructure, pipelines, deployment, monitoring and experimentation interfaces.
Traditional ML/DL roles were fewer than 2 percent and resembled ML Engineer or Research Engineer work.
The proposed definition centered on owning the design, evaluation and production operation of foundation-model systems.
Roles were 95.6 percent production-focused, nearly 50 percent backend-heavy and about 20 percent often full-stack.
RAG appeared in 35.9 percent, prompt engineering in 29.1 percent, LLM integration in 25.4 percent, agents in 14.4 percent and fine-tuning in 8.5 percent.
Python appeared in 82.5 percent, TypeScript in 23.4 percent, React in 14.8 percent and FastAPI in 10.7 percent.
Operations and cloud appeared in 17.4 percent and 13.4 percent; AWS, Docker, CI/CD and Kubernetes were the leading infrastructure mentions.
Classical ML was 9.5 percent overall, with PyTorch at 22.0 percent within that group and TensorFlow at 12.9 percent.
LangChain, LangGraph and LlamaIndex were present but no single GenAI framework dominated.
unsupported_claims_removed: Removed claims that would treat this dataset's percentages as an eternal or universal definition of AI Engineering.
Removed unsupported hiring predictions and personal anecdotes not present in the market study.
substantive_edits: Rewrote the study as a first-person account of the analysis and its interpretation.
Grouped the exact percentages by role category, GenAI skills, application layer, operations and frameworks.
Preserved the distinction between the study's observed market signals and the proposed practical definition.
